pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–11; understand the CAUSES (cattle ranching — the biggest Amazon driver — plus soy, palm oil, logging, mining) and the SCALE of deforestation (~10 million hectares/year), and its impact on biodiversity, climate and indigenous peoples.
• Standards — UK: DfE KS2 Geography (land use, economic activity, distribution of natural resources) and Science Y6 'human impact on environments'; leads to KS3 'Earth and atmosphere'.
• Standards — US: NGSS 5-ESS3-1 and MS-ESS3-3/-4 (human activities affecting Earth's systems; managing human impact).
• Operational details — teach causes as an ECONOMIC chain (demand → land cleared for a cash crop/pasture → forest lost), naming cattle as the Amazon's largest single driver. On scale, the taxonomy's '~10 million hectares/year' is essentially right: FAO FRA 2025 gives GROSS deforestation of 10.9 Mha/year (2015–2025), down from 17.6 Mha in the 1990s; teach it as 'about the size of a country like Portugal/Iceland every year, though the rate is now falling'. Distinguish for stronger pupils: gross deforestation (~10.9 Mha) vs NET forest change (~4.1 Mha after regrowth), and 'deforestation' (permanent) vs temporary tree-cover loss (fire/logging that regrows). Link three impacts: biodiversity (habitat gone), climate (stored carbon released), indigenous peoples (homes and rights lost).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (9): name three causes. Tier B (10): state the ~10 million ha/year scale and explain two impacts. Tier C (11): trace a driver (beef/soy/palm) to forest loss and distinguish gross vs net loss or permanent vs temporary clearance.
bestPractices: Frame causes as an economic chain: demand → land cleared for a product → forest lost, with cattle named as the Amazon's biggest single driver.
Make the scale concrete by comparing ~10 Mha/year to a familiar country's area, and note the rate is now falling (avoid a doom-only framing).
Distinguish gross deforestation from net loss, and permanent deforestation from temporary tree-cover loss that regrows, for higher-attaining pupils.
Tie each impact to a mechanism (habitat destroyed → biodiversity; carbon released → climate; land taken → indigenous peoples).
Use up-to-date figures (FRA 2025) rather than older round numbers, and cite the source.
keyRepresentations: A land-use map/dashboard with drivers (cattle, soy, palm, logging, mining) and live forest/biodiversity/carbon meters.
A scale comparison: 10 Mha ≈ the area of a named country, shown against a map.
Before/after satellite imagery of a cleared region.
commonMisconceptions: 'Deforestation is mostly people chopping wood for firewood' — the big drivers are commercial cattle, soy, palm oil, logging and mining.
'The whole rainforest will be gone next year' — the scale is huge but it is a percentage per year, and the rate is currently falling.
'Tree-cover loss and deforestation are the same' — some loss (fire, selective logging) regrows; deforestation is permanent land-use change.
'It only harms animals' — it also releases carbon (climate) and displaces indigenous communities.
'Trees just grow back quickly' — cleared rainforest on thin soil often does not recover its biodiversity.

learn.summary: For ages 9–11, this guidance teaches the CAUSES of rainforest deforestation as an economic chain (demand → land cleared for a cash product → forest lost), with cattle ranching named as the Amazon's single largest driver, alongside soy, palm oil, logging and mining. It teaches the SCALE (gross deforestation ~10–11 million hectares worldwide per year, made concrete by comparison to a familiar country's area, with the note that the rate is currently falling) and links three impacts via their mechanisms: habitat loss → biodiversity, carbon release → climate, land taken → indigenous peoples. A manipulable land-use model is the lead activity; a reveal infographic, a sort-and-estimate practice task, an optional 3D flythrough, and (deferred) stakeholder dialogue are preserved as alternatives with distinct purposes.

activities.title: Land-use control panel: build the forest loss from ordinary demands
feedback: When a learner clears only one driver, point out which drivers they haven't yet accounted for and that cattle is the single biggest Amazon driver.
When the running total approaches the scale figure, anchor it to the country-area comparison and clarify that ~10 million ha/year is the WORLDWIDE annual total, not the loss of one region alone.

When regrowth/protection is toggled, highlight two separate ideas: protection reduces how much is cleared each year (gross loss), and regrowth makes net loss smaller than gross loss. Add that the real worldwide deforestation rate is high but has slowed in recent decades, so avoid a 'gone next year' reading.

If a learner treats all cleared land as permanently lost, use the regrowth toggle to distinguish temporary tree-cover loss (fire, selective logging) from permanent land-use change; add that cleared rainforest on thin soil often does not recover its original biodiversity even where some regrowth occurs.
activities.rationale: A drivers→consequences system is well suited to a manipulable model where cause-and-effect allocation is visible: allocating land and seeing forest, biodiversity, carbon and community meters respond may build a systems intuition that static facts alone do not. Live meters and the gross-vs-net toggle are concrete mechanisms intended to make the economic chain and the scale trend felt, not just stated. This is a research-informed proposal, not a tested intervention; the live-meter and toggle examples are illustrative, not mandatory.
sourceClaims: Global GROSS deforestation is 10.9 million hectares per year for 2015–2025, down from 17.6 million ha/year in 1990–2000; net forest loss is about 4.12 million ha/year after accounting for forest expansion

Tropical primary rainforest loss was about 4.3 million hectares in 2025 (a record 6.7 Mha in 2024); cattle ranching is the largest single driver of Amazon deforestation, with soy, palm oil, logging and mining also major causes
learnerActions: Play the role of a developer on a map of a rainforest region: allocate patches of land to cattle pasture to meet beef demand, then add soy and palm plots, then logging and mining.
Watch linked meters recompute live as you clear land — forest area falls, a biodiversity/species meter drops, a CO2-released gauge climbs, and a marker shows a displaced community.

Play a year-timeline forward and watch the forest visibly shrink while a running total ticks upward; note that the worldwide annual total is about 10 million hectares a year, so the regional model shows how such demands accumulate.
Compare that worldwide annual total to a familiar country's area (e.g. roughly the size of Portugal or Iceland).

Switch on a second set of controls — regrowth and protected areas — and watch protected areas reduce how much forest is cleared each year (gross loss), while regrowth makes NET loss smaller than gross loss; note that the real worldwide deforestation rate has slowed over recent decades but is still high.
activities.intendedInsight: Deforestation is not random destruction but the sum of ordinary DEMANDS — beef, soy, palm, timber, minerals — each trading a patch of irreplaceable forest for a product; the totals are staggering yet changeable, and gross loss differs from net loss once regrowth is counted.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal driver infographic with before/after and scale comparison
feedback: If a learner expects firewood-gathering to dominate, reveal the commercial driver shares to correct it.
Reinforce that cattle ranching is the largest single Amazon driver when learners rank the causes.
activities.rationale: A reveal infographic delivers the causes and the scale statistic memorably and may support learners who need the facts anchored before modelling trade-offs. It conveys shares and mechanism clearly, though it does not itself let pupils explore the trade-offs a manipulable model can.
sourceClaims: Global GROSS deforestation is 10.9 million hectares per year for 2015–2025, down from 17.6 million ha/year in 1990–2000; net forest loss is about 4.12 million ha/year after accounting for forest expansion

Tropical primary rainforest loss was about 4.3 million hectares in 2025 (a record 6.7 Mha in 2024); cattle ranching is the largest single driver of Amazon deforestation, with soy, palm oil, logging and mining also major causes
learnerActions: Tap each driver hotspot (cattle, soy, palm oil, logging, mining) to reveal its share and the mechanism by which it clears forest.
Swipe a before/after satellite pair of a cleared region to see the change directly.
Study a scale visual showing '≈10.9 Mha worldwide per year = an area this big' set against a map of a familiar country.
activities.intendedInsight: In the Amazon and many tropical regions the major drivers are commercial land uses producing for national and export markets (not mainly firewood), and the annual worldwide scale is enormous but comparable to a real country's footprint.

activities.title: Sort the causes and estimate the annual scale
feedback: On the firewood distractor, redirect to the large commercial drivers clearing land for profit and export.
On the slider, give the real figure and the country-area comparison rather than only marking right/wrong.

For the regrowth-vs-ranch item, confirm that under the common definition used for the ~10 million ha figure, permanent conversion to farmland is deforestation while temporary loss that regrows is not, so not all tree-cover loss is permanent — and note thin-soil rainforest often does not recover its original biodiversity.
activities.rationale: Categorisation, estimation and mechanism-matching map cleanly onto the three evidence points and give clean practice and checking. A sort or match can teach and check classification but does not by itself elicit independent construction of the economic chain, so pupils are also asked to state the chain in their own words.
sourceClaims: Global GROSS deforestation is 10.9 million hectares per year for 2015–2025, down from 17.6 million ha/year in 1990–2000; net forest loss is about 4.12 million ha/year after accounting for forest expansion

Tropical primary rainforest loss was about 4.3 million hectares in 2025 (a record 6.7 Mha in 2024); cattle ranching is the largest single driver of Amazon deforestation, with soy, palm oil, logging and mining also major causes
learnerActions: Sort a set of cards into the main commercial drivers of Amazon and tropical deforestation (cattle, soy, palm, logging, mining) versus minor causes like 'villagers gathering firewood'.
Use a slider to estimate how many hectares of forest are lost worldwide each year, then compare your estimate against the real figure (~10–11 million ha/year gross worldwide).
Answer short questions matching each impact to its mechanism: habitat loss → biodiversity, carbon release → climate, land taken → indigenous peoples.
Decide whether two scenarios are both 'deforestation': a patch logged that regrows over 30 years versus a patch turned permanently into a cattle ranch — and explain why.
State the driver→product→forest-loss chain in your own words for one driver.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can identify the dominant commercial drivers, place the annual worldwide scale, and distinguish permanent deforestation from temporary tree-cover loss that regrows.

activities.title: Optional: 3D flythrough over cleared vs intact forest
feedback: If learners focus only on the visual drama, link it back to which demands drove the clearance and to the scale figures from the other activities.
activities.rationale: A 3D flythrough may make the contrast between cleared and intact forest visceral. The drivers-and-quantities learning is also carried by the 2D map/model, so this is an optional enrichment rather than the core, and is practical only where a reusable terrain asset already exists. No claim is made that 3D is more or less effective than the 2D model; efficacy is untested.
learnerActions: View or navigate a 3D flythrough that passes over cleared land beside intact rainforest to see the contrast directly.
Relate what you see to the drivers and quantities studied in the other activities — which demands drove this clearance, and how it adds to the annual total.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing cleared versus intact forest in 3D can make the loss vivid, while the core learning remains the drivers and quantities behind it.

activities.title: Optional: competing stakeholders (deferred extension)
feedback: Where learners cast one group as the sole cause, surface the chain of demand connecting consumers, producers and land clearance.
activities.rationale: Multi-stakeholder dialogue may surface competing motives, but that debate belongs to a downstream 'Futures & Trade-Offs' topic; at this stage the goal is understanding causes and scale, so keep this as an optional extension rather than the core.
learnerActions: Hear from or role-play a rancher, a logger and a conservationist, each stating their motives for and against clearing forest.
Identify the competing demands and trade-offs behind a single cleared patch.
activities.intendedInsight: Behind forest loss sit real people with competing economic motives; deforestation decisions involve trade-offs, not simple villains.

constraints: Core objective is understanding causes (as an economic demand chain) and scale, plus linking three impacts to mechanisms — not stakeholder debate, which is a later topic.

Sort/estimate/match formats can teach and check classification and recall, but recognition-only tasks do not by themselves elicit independent construction of the economic chain; have learners state the driver→product→forest-loss chain in their own words.

The reveal infographic, sort/estimate task and 3D flythrough are scaffolds; they do not let learners explore trade-offs the way the manipulable model does, and no medium is asserted as universally superior.
Avoid a doom-only framing: state that the rate is high but currently falling, and distinguish gross deforestation from net loss and permanent deforestation from temporary tree-cover loss.
Present the ~10 million ha/year figure as approximate and as a WORLDWIDE annual total, and cite up-to-date sources rather than older round numbers.
Address the misconception that 'trees just grow back': cleared rainforest on thin soil often does not recover its original biodiversity, even where some regrowth occurs.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Figure reconciliation: the pedagogy/evidence state '~10 million hectares/year' while FAO FRA 2025 gives gross ~10.9 Mha/year (2015–2025) and net ~4.12 Mha/year; these are consistent if '10 million' is read as the approximate GROSS worldwide figure. Activities use '~10–11 million ha/year gross' and explicitly contrast net loss to avoid conflating the two.
The ~10 million ha/year figure is global; the lead model depicts one rainforest region, so feedback explicitly clarifies the total is worldwide to avoid implying a single region loses that amount.

The WRI/Global Forest Watch source (cattle as largest Amazon driver; tropical primary forest loss figures) is marked verified:false in the row; the DfE curriculum source is also verified:false. Treat the cattle-as-largest-driver and 2024/2025 primary-loss figures as unverified at the time of this rewrite.

The row's 'ideal'/'strong'/'possible' fit language and claims that the model conveys the learning 'fully' or that 3D 'adds nothing' were not treated as established efficacy claims; the 3D flythrough alternative is retained with scoped affordances and limits, using proposed/may wording where efficacy is untested.
Country-area comparisons (Portugal/Iceland) are approximate illustrations of scale, not precise equivalences; present them as rough visual anchors.

probeDeeper: Which single activity clears the most Amazon rainforest?
About how much forest is lost worldwide each year?
Name two different kinds of harm deforestation causes beyond losing trees.
A patch is logged and grows back over 30 years; another is turned into a permanent cattle ranch. Are both 'deforestation'? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: No — firewood-gathering is not the main cause. Most large-scale deforestation is commercial: clearing land for cattle ranching (the biggest driver in the Amazon), soy and palm oil plantations, logging for timber, and mining — clearing huge areas for profit and export. Roughly 10 million hectares of forest are lost worldwide each year, harming biodiversity, the climate, and indigenous communities.

errorPatterns.pattern: deforestation is mostly firewood / poor locals — 'villagers cutting trees for cooking'
errorPatterns.nextMove: point to the large commercial drivers (cattle, soy, palm, logging, mining) clearing land for profit and export
errorPatterns.distractor: It's mostly poor villagers cutting trees for firewood
errorPatterns.revealedBy: names subsistence firewood as the main cause

errorPatterns.pattern: any tree loss is permanent deforestation — doesn't distinguish permanent clearing from forest that regrows
errorPatterns.nextMove: distinguish permanent conversion to farmland from temporary loss that can regrow
errorPatterns.revealedBy: treats all tree-cover loss (including regrowth after fire or logging) as permanent deforestation

errorPatterns.pattern: deforestation only hurts trees and animals — misses climate and indigenous communities
errorPatterns.nextMove: add carbon release (climate) and displacement of indigenous peoples

responseLevels.gap: Blames firewood or vague 'people'; no sense of commercial drivers or scale.
responseLevels.full: Names the major commercial drivers (cattle largest in the Amazon, plus soy, palm, logging, mining), states the ~10 million hectares/year scale, and explains impacts across biodiversity, climate and indigenous communities.
responseLevels.partial: Names one or two real drivers or the scale figure, but not the dominant commercial causes or the range of impacts.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A lot of people think rainforests are mostly cut down by poor villagers gathering firewood. Is that the main cause of large-scale deforestation? Tell me yes or no, then tell me what the biggest causes really are and WHY.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child blaming small-scale firewood or local poverty misidentifies the driver; the concept child names the big COMMERCIAL, export-driven causes (cattle/soy/palm/logging/mining) and the global scale. The reason-tier forces the profit-and-scale reasoning.
